rv.q: This is a highly accessible and entertaining rendition of this rarely produced drama.
Mr. Gaines takes confident advantage of this prized chance, giving a sterling performance that allows us to see Dr. Stockmann from all the perspectives Ibsen intended.
Clearly, MTC has lucked out with its timing of this classic drama, its Victorian-era polemics ordinarily a bit simplistic — but given the peculiar insanity of election politics, right on the money.
Nor does it make sense that they would object to Sam Gold’s crackling and persuasive production, which drove those views home despite having to regroup once the protesters were ejected.
Don't be put off by any grumbles about the conversational, tightened two-hour adaptation

Rebecca Lenkiewicz's "new version" of "An Enemy of the People" is yet another attempt to update Henrik Ibsen's smug 1882 satire about a visionary doctor (Boyd Gaines) who becomes a pariah when he makes a discovery that threatens to gut the economy of the hypocriticAl Small town in which he lives.
But this 1882 play by Ibsen, a pioneer in realism, has never seemed more simplistic and black-and-white than in this version.
It's a tall task; Enemy plays as an all-words white-knuckle thriller without so much as a gun to raise the stakes.
In a riveting production by Rebecca Lenkiewicz at the Manhattan Theatre Club, Boyd Gaines plays Dr. Thomas Stockmann who insists on telling the truth though it may cost his livelihood.

cn.t: This rollicking, streamlined revival makes Ibsen's 1882 drama feel urgent and timely, though some critics find the production lacks restraint and can't fully overcome the play's inherent didacticism.
